strengths: The paper identifies a timely and important evaluation gap: standard math and coding benchmarks may conceal failures caused specifically by parallel token decoding in diffusion LLMs.

The conditional-total-correlation formulation provides a clean conceptual account of the speed–quality trade-off. The multi-step decomposition, monotonicity result, and analytically tractable list-operation examples form a coherent theoretical narrative.

ParallelBench covers 17 tasks with controllable difficulty, and the experiments span several open and closed diffusion models, autoregressive models, unmasking rules, semi-autoregressive decoding, fine-tuning, chain-of-thought prompting, caching, and remasking.

The empirical contrasts among Copy/Replace Index, Replace Random, and Shuffle are informative and generally consistent with the theory. The paper is clearly organized and includes useful prompts, training details, complete plots, and illustrative failure cases.
weaknesses: The benchmark is presented as realistic, but much of it consists of synthetic list operations wrapped in a waiting-line narrative, generated word sets, and small 4x4 puzzles. Consequently, the evidence does not yet establish that the reported limitations are consequential across representative real-world applications.

The evaluation does not measure actual latency, throughput, or hardware efficiency. Tokens decoded per step is only a proxy for speed and ignores denoiser cost, sequence padding, caching behavior, and implementation overhead, weakening the central speed–quality claims.

Several evaluation choices are fragile: most tasks have only about 100 examples, no confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are reported, and text quality is primarily represented by a binary automatic grammar checker without human evaluation. Task-specific semantic metrics are not consistently used in the main trade-off analysis.

The strongest causal interpretations are not fully controlled. Comparisons between diffusion and autoregressive models conflate architecture, scale, training data, tokenization, and instruction-following ability; Mercury's decoding policy is unknown, so its errors cannot confidently be attributed to parallel decoding.

The theoretical results are useful but fairly direct extensions of the known one-step factorization bound, assume fixed irreversible partitions and unrestricted ideal marginals, and establish KL error rather than the downstream accuracy degradation emphasized experimentally. The paper should more clearly delimit their applicability to practical and revisable diffusion decoders.

Directly relevant recent adaptive approaches discussed in the related-work section, such as entropy-bounded, dilated, and SlowFast sampling, are not evaluated. This makes the broad conclusion about the limitations of current parallel decoding strategies incomplete.

The oracle selects thresholds retrospectively using ground-truth correctness and is therefore unattainable; it demonstrates hindsight headroom but does not by itself show that a learnable adaptive policy can realize the claimed improvement. Reproducibility is also weakened by the blank project-page entry and lack of an accessible benchmark/code link in the manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important question: whether the advertised inference advantages of diffusion LLMs survive once generation quality is measured on tasks with strong output dependencies.

The conditional-total-correlation formulation provides a useful conceptual lens, and the analytically tractable list tasks make the core failure mode easy to understand. The synthetic experiments broadly support the predicted trends.

The empirical study covers multiple diffusion LLMs, unmasking strategies, autoregressive baselines, KV caching, fine-tuning, remasking, chain-of-thought prompting, and two discrete-diffusion parameterizations.

weaknesses: The central “realistic benchmark” claim is not convincing. Most Waiting Line tasks are synthetic list manipulations wrapped in a customer-service narrative, while Words-to-Sentence and 4x4 puzzles are similarly artificial. The evaluation therefore demonstrates constructed failure modes more clearly than practically important real-world limitations.

There are serious benchmark-quality problems. The one-shot Sort example is incorrectly sorted by last name, and the Latin Square example requests a square of size 3 while supplying four symbols and expecting a 4x4 answer. These inconsistent demonstrations can directly alter model behavior; the near-universal zero Sort scores further suggest that this is not merely cosmetic.

The Text Writing metrics do not adequately establish output quality. A binary grammar checker is used for the main curves, summarization can receive a high primary score without preserving content, and Words-to-Sentence accuracy only checks inclusion of requested words. There is no human validation of grammaticality, coherence, or semantic fidelity.

Despite repeatedly framing the results as a speed-quality trade-off, the paper primarily uses tokens unmasked per step as a speed proxy. It does not report wall-clock latency, throughput, denoiser calls under comparable implementations, or hardware-normalized speedups. This is especially problematic when comparing adaptive decoding, KV caching, longer chain-of-thought outputs, and different model architectures.

The theory is limited relative to the claims. The KL decomposition and monotonicity result are fairly direct consequences of conditional total correlation and factorization. More importantly, conditional total correlation is never estimated for the realistic tasks; assertions that W2S-hard has larger correlation than W2S-easy, or that observed task orderings validate the theory, remain qualitative speculation confounded by model capacity and prompt difficulty.

The proof of Theorem 2 assumes that the last set of an optimal T-step partition can be split into two nonempty subsets, which need not hold. The theorem may be repairable by splitting any non-singleton set and carefully accounting for later conditioning, but the stated proof is incomplete.

The oracle analysis uses hindsight to choose, per sample, the least expensive threshold producing a correct answer. This is an unrealizable selection rule and mainly shows that different thresholds sometimes work; it does not demonstrate that an adaptive method could identify them from information available at inference time.

Cross-model comparisons are difficult to interpret because model scale, training, decoding configurations, and output budgets are not controlled. Mercury's internal parallelism is unknown, while open-source dLLMs are fixed to a particular setting and autoregressive systems differ substantially in capacity. These comparisons cannot isolate decoding architecture as the cause of performance differences.

The experiments use only about 100 examples per task and provide no uncertainty estimates, significance tests, sensitivity to prompts or seeds, or human assessment. Dataset generation also relies on unspecified Gemini outputs. Together with the apparent prompt errors, this substantially weakens reliability and reproducibility.

Overall, the paper identifies a genuine phenomenon but overstates the novelty, realism, and practical implications of its evidence. The invalid benchmark examples, weak quality metrics, and absence of actual speed measurements are major issues rather than minor omissions.

strengths: Timely and important problem: the paper directly examines the defining speed–quality trade-off of parallel decoding in diffusion LLMs, which standard math and coding benchmarks may not expose.

The information-theoretic treatment provides a clear conceptual framework. The KL lower bound, monotonicity result, and analytically tractable list operations connect token dependence, decoding steps, and attainable quality.

The empirical study is broad, covering multiple open- and closed-source diffusion models, autoregressive models, static and adaptive unmasking strategies, semi-autoregressive decoding, KV caching, fine-tuning, chain-of-thought prompting, remasking, and an alternative diffusion transition process.

The contrast between deterministic/index-based operations and random/permutation operations is insightful and consistently supported by synthetic analysis, controlled fine-tuning, realistic task variants, and illustrative failure cases.
PARALLELBENCH fills a useful evaluation gap by including tasks with controllable difficulty and by emphasizing adaptation of parallelism rather than performance at a single decoding configuration.
The manuscript is clearly written, visually polished, and unusually thorough in its appendices, with prompts, dataset sizes, evaluation protocols, training details, and complete model-level results.
weaknesses: The benchmark is described as realistic, but much of it remains synthetic or toy-like: Waiting Line is a natural-language wrapper around list manipulation, Words-to-Sentence is artificially constructed, and the puzzles are only 4×4. Evidence on genuinely deployed, long-form applications is limited.

The central speed–quality claims primarily use average tokens decoded per step as a proxy for speed. Actual latency, throughput, denoiser calls, memory use, and hardware-normalized wall-clock measurements are not reported, although caching and variable sequence lengths can make tokens-per-step an imperfect efficiency measure.

The theory assumes a specified partition of output variables at each step. Practical confidence-based strategies select positions adaptively from model predictions; such selection can be dependent on the predicted values. The input-dependent extension does not fully establish that the same lower bound directly characterizes these model- and history-dependent selection mechanisms.

For natural-language tasks, conditional total correlation is not estimated. Assertions that paraphrasing, easy W2S, and hard W2S have progressively larger dependency are plausible but inferred from task design and observed degradation, so model error and distributional dependence are not cleanly separated.

The language evaluation is weak for several stated claims. Binary LanguageTool grammaticality does not reliably assess fluency or coherence, and the main plots label this quantity as accuracy. Human evaluation or stronger learned judgments would substantially strengthen the natural-language findings.

Most benchmark subsets contain only 100 examples, yet the paper provides no confidence intervals, variability across seeds, or significance tests. This is particularly relevant for stochastic tasks, threshold selection, and relatively small differences between decoding strategies.

The oracle chooses a successful threshold separately for each evaluated sample using outcome knowledge. It is useful as an existence illustration but may benefit from repeated candidate selection and does not by itself show that a realizable adaptive policy can approach the displayed trade-off.

The theoretical results are elegant but largely follow from standard KL factorization and total-correlation identities, making the theoretical novelty moderate. Reproducibility also depends on releasing the generated benchmark instances and evaluation code, since several datasets were produced using an external proprietary model.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely evaluation gap: standard reasoning and coding benchmarks do not isolate the speed–quality failure modes specific to parallel decoding.

The conditional-total-correlation formulation provides a useful conceptual account of why simultaneously generated tokens can be individually plausible but jointly inconsistent. The boundary cases and synthetic list-operation calculations make the phenomenon intuitive and quantitatively interpretable.

PARALLELBENCH covers 17 tasks with controllable difficulty and includes useful contrasts between deterministic tasks and tasks with multiple valid outputs, such as Replace Index versus Replace Random and Sudoku versus Latin Square.

The empirical study is unusually broad: it evaluates several open and closed diffusion LLMs, autoregressive baselines, multiple static and adaptive unmasking rules, semi-autoregressive decoding, caching, fine-tuning, chain-of-thought, remasking, alternative diffusion transitions, and recent decoding methods.

The principal empirical finding is convincing: accuracy can collapse quickly as parallelism increases, while confidence-threshold methods improve but do not eliminate the trade-off. Fine-tuning experiments further help separate model-capacity errors from distribution-induced dependence errors.

The appendix reports sample counts, prompts, metrics, training hyperparameters, longer-output experiments, supplementary metrics, and wall-clock latency measurements, providing a reasonably strong basis for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The claimed “realistic” scope is overstated. Ten of the 17 tasks are synthetic, templated waiting-line transformations; three are LLM-generated word-combination tasks; and the two puzzles are small 4x4 instances. These are useful diagnostic stress tests, but limited evidence for broad real-world behavior.

The theory mainly formalizes a known factorization limitation through a fairly direct conditional-total-correlation decomposition. It applies to monotone decoding with fixed or input-dependent partitions and no later token revision; it does not directly establish an unavoidable limitation for all diffusion-LLM samplers, especially generation-dependent partitions, remasking, or iterative refinement. Several statements generalize beyond this formal scope.

The proof of Theorem 2 says the final set of an optimal partition can be split into two nonempty sets, although that set may be a singleton. The argument appears repairable by splitting any nonsingleton set and retaining subsequent sets, but the presented proof is incomplete.

The task-characterization methodology in Section F.1 is internally inconsistent. The stated center-of-mass formula assigns smaller values to tasks whose performance collapses at low parallelism, yet the text and figure place harder-to-parallelize tasks to the right. Likewise, the interpretation of a fitted slope versus block length appears sign-reversed. This undermines Figure 6's reproducibility and conclusions.

Each task has only about 100 examples, with no uncertainty intervals, repeated decoding seeds, or statistical tests. This is particularly concerning for randomized prompts, temperature-based infilling, small differences between methods, and claims about ordering tasks by difficulty.

The primary text-generation measure is a binary score from an automatic grammar checker. It is not validated against human judgments and does not measure coherence, factuality, semantic preservation, or overall generation quality. The supplementary ROUGE-L and BERTScore results degrade much less, weakening broad claims of severe text-quality deterioration.

“Tokens per step” is only a proxy for speed and can obscure different sequence lengths and per-step computational costs. Wall-clock validation is limited to one model, one GPU configuration, and aggregated results, so the claimed inference trade-offs are not comprehensively established.

The oracle selects a threshold post hoc using knowledge of which output is correct. It is a useful diagnostic of headroom, but it is neither an implementable method nor a rigorous upper bound over decoding strategies; describing it as the best possible trade-off is too strong.

Comparisons to autoregressive models are not fully controlled for model family, scale, training data, or decoding protocol, and Mercury's internal parallelism is unknown. These results are illustrative but cannot cleanly attribute differences to autoregressive versus diffusion modeling.

strengths: The paper studies a timely and practically important question: when parallel decoding in diffusion language models actually provides useful speedups without sacrificing quality.

The synthetic list-operation analysis gives intuitive examples of how factorized parallel predictions violate global constraints. The conditional-total-correlation formulation provides a useful conceptual lens, even if much of the derivation is fairly direct.

The empirical scope is broad: several open- and closed-source diffusion models, multiple unmasking strategies, semi-autoregressive decoding, caching, fine-tuning, remasking, alternative diffusion transitions, recent adaptive decoders, and wall-clock latency are considered.

The benchmark includes controllable task variants and clearly separates deterministic operations from operations with multiple valid outputs. Prompts, sample counts, metrics, and many implementation details are documented in the appendix.
The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and visually polished.
weaknesses: The claimed connection between conditional total correlation and the realistic benchmark is largely asserted rather than established. Conditional total correlation is computed only for idealized atomic list operations; it is neither measured nor credibly estimated for the natural-language tasks. Labels such as low, high, and very high dependency are assigned qualitatively and then supported using the same performance trends they are meant to explain, creating a circular argument.

The benchmark is described as realistic and as containing tasks trivial for autoregressive LLMs, but much of it consists of artificial templated list manipulation, generated word sets, and small puzzles. The reported autoregressive results directly undermine the latter claim: several strong models obtain approximately 0% on sorting and 0–21% on Sudoku, and many perform poorly on indexed insertion and removal. Thus, model capability and instruction-following failures remain substantial confounders.

The natural-language evaluation is not convincing enough to support claims of severe generation-quality degradation. The main metric is a binary LanguageTool grammar judgment without human validation or an analysis of false positives and negatives. Inclusion accuracy does not measure coherence, while ROUGE-L and BERTScore degrade only mildly with parallelism. No human evaluation assesses fluency, semantic preservation, or overall usefulness.

The theoretical contribution is limited in novelty relative to prior work already identifying conditional-independence errors and task-dependent parallelizability. The main lower bound is essentially a stepwise application of the standard total-correlation projection onto factorized distributions. Moreover, the proof of monotonicity as written assumes that the final set of an optimal partition can be split into two nonempty subsets; an optimal partition may instead have a singleton final set. The result may be repairable by splitting another nonsingleton set, but the presented proof is incomplete.

The central conclusions overgeneralize from a restricted decoder class. The analysis assumes tokens finalized in the same step are sampled independently and cannot subsequently be revised. It therefore establishes a limitation of that factorized, irreversible decoding procedure, not parallel decoding or diffusion LLMs broadly. Joint verification, structured decoding, and learned iterative refinement fall outside the theorem.

The experimental evidence lacks basic uncertainty reporting. Most tasks use only 100 examples, yet there are no confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance tests despite many comparisons and sometimes small differences. Dataset generation with Gemini is only briefly described, with no human quality-control or contamination analysis.

The hindsight oracle chooses the best threshold separately for each test sample using knowledge of evaluation success. It shows an upper envelope for a fixed threshold family, but does not demonstrate that a realizable adaptive policy can identify those thresholds. Describing its gap as evidence that per-sample adaptation alone yields significant attainable improvement is too strong.

Cross-model comparisons are difficult to interpret because model sizes, training objectives, instruction tuning, output settings, and decoding controls differ; Mercury's internal parallelism is unknown. Consequently, these comparisons cannot cleanly attribute performance differences to parallel decoding.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the manuscript contains blank project, leaderboard, and repository fields, and does not provide the benchmark instances, evaluation scripts, generated-name pools, exact sampled subsets, or uncertainty-producing protocols within the submission. Overall, the paper has a useful diagnostic idea and substantial experimentation, but the benchmark validity and central explanatory claims are not sufficiently supported for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper identifies a timely and practically important failure mode: parallel unmasking can lose dependencies among simultaneously generated tokens, directly challenging current diffusion-LLM acceleration claims.
The conditional-total-correlation perspective is useful, and the analytically tractable list operations yield concrete predictions that are empirically validated after fine-tuning.

PARALLELBENCH spans varied dependency structures and exposes failures obscured by aggregate math and coding benchmarks. Contrasts such as Replace Index versus Replace Random and Sudoku versus Latin Square are intuitive and diagnostic.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering multiple open and closed diffusion LLMs, autoregressive controls, static and adaptive unmasking, semi-autoregressive decoding, KV caching, fine-tuning, chain-of-thought, remasking, recent parallel decoders, longer outputs, and Medusa. A100 latency measurements also supplement tokens-per-step results.
The manuscript is clear and well organized, with informative failure cases and substantial experimental appendices. The proposed benchmark could become a useful diagnostic resource.
weaknesses: The benchmark is described as realistic, but much of it remains synthetic or highly templated: Waiting Line wraps list operations in natural language, W2S uses LLM-generated word sets, and the puzzles are small 4x4 instances. This supports controlled diagnosis but weakens claims about real-world prevalence and impact.

The connection between conditional total correlation and several empirical conclusions is heuristic. C(Y|X) is not estimated for text tasks, yet qualitative dependency levels are assigned and used to explain their degradation. Model capacity, tokenization, output length, decoding order, and metric behavior remain plausible confounders.

Text-generation conclusions rely heavily on a binary LanguageTool grammar score without human validation or robustness analysis. Semantic and content metrics often degrade less. The approximately 100 samples per task and absence of confidence intervals, repeated-run variability, or significance testing further limit the evidential strength.

Section F.1 contains an apparent inconsistency: its center-of-mass definition implies that rapid degradation produces a smaller parallelizability value and explicitly says smaller is harder, whereas Figure 6 and the main text place harder tasks to the right. Either an unreported transformation was applied or the axis interpretation is reversed.

The proof of Theorem 2 has a gap because it splits the last block of an optimal partition, although that block may be a singleton while an earlier block is nonsingleton. The result likely can be repaired by splitting a nonsingleton block in place, but the submitted proof is incomplete. The theoretical contribution is otherwise a relatively direct extension of a known factorization bound.

The oracle selects a threshold using correctness outcomes for each sample. It is a useful headroom diagnostic, but it is neither an achievable decoder nor a general upper bound over adaptive methods, so conclusions about realizable per-sample adaptation are overstated.

Speed evidence is narrower than quality evidence. Tokens per step is only a proxy, while wall-clock results cover one model, one GPU, batch size one, and an aggregate score; throughput, batching, memory, and cross-model latency are not studied.
